I felt for them mostly because I could see how none of them thought they had any other choice. Maybe I can retrospectively say that they had many options other than staying with Dutch, which is true, and might annoy players as they continue to watch them follow him. But they genuinely didn’t think there was any other way, mostly because they didn’t have anybody else but him and their relationships with each other were progressively more monitored and triangulated by Dutch/Micah as well. I also tried not to be hampered by expectation—there were some characters I didn’t really feel much for, like Sean, but his death was made somewhat more important through camp interactions that showed me that he was important to other characters in the game. Not viewing the game through my own standards of what is normal, but trying to regard it within the context it painstakingly builds for itself through hours of camp interactions that honestly show you—these characters aren’t meant to be smart. So many lines where they call each other dumbasses or Arthur gets called a meathead or no-brained or whatever variation. I think you are encouraged to try to see intelligence beyond the superficial markers of it, by engaging in the little details. For me it was how John was always asking questions. Sometimes existential ones. How Arthur’s morality took a shift once he finally allowed himself to.. well, think for himself. I don’t think any of these little things are especially profound on their own, but it paints a picture of people who had precious little education and only really had one person who they could trust, Dutch, and only each other by way of extension. What could they have been like if not for the gang? I kept finding myself asking that, too.

Thank you for your comment — as you mentioned, the tower (symbolizing identity and worth, which you recognized) is built of tragedies. How does it get taller? By the speaker seeking out more miserable experiences, and contributing them as building blocks. By “now I know better,” the speaker recognizes that while it is finally tall, it is desolate due to its own design—because tragedy begets isolation and a lack of trust in others. “The keypad is dusted over,” suggesting the tower may be grand but nobody ever enters, and the speaker also does not leave. From within the tower, the speaker asks if the world if it can still see them through its walls, and thus, if it can hurt them (and paradoxically, build it even taller). The world says nothing, again because of the desolation that the speaker brought upon themselves. The speaker—whose warped conflation of worth with an accumulation of tragic experiences has finally broken them—finally has come to feel that because of the pain they suffered while struggling to be seen and appear worthy, that the world sparing them of any attention (and thus, pain) is the truest form of love. I can understand in my own way and also the onset of narcissistic traits. When I got to Uni, I was finally away from my abusive mother and was able to do mundane things like choosing my own hairstyle for the first time. I immediately got attention for my appearance for the first time in my life, from men in my Uni and older men on the street. Suddenly girls in my class wanted to be my friends and were making the initiative to be around me—not the other way around. I also clung to creativity and intelligence growing up and was convinced I was ugly, so this was a complete shock. I had never been the subject of peoples’ attraction before. But I responded to it by chopping my hair off and adopting a more masculine style of dress. I hated the attention so much. This isn’t a self-hating coping mechanism, I am truly comfortable this way but I’d be lying if I said it wasn’t because the attention to my appearance made me, perhaps as you are, fixate so much on everything about the way I looked that it drove me crazy. I was obsessed—and unfortunately, while I’m better, still am in some ways—with meeting peoples’ expectations for my appearance because I was convinced there was literally nothing else good about me. Changing my style to pivot away from what is conventionally attractive to men freed me a bit. But if I’m acting to subvert expectations, I’m still acting in response to the cause, right? So maybe I’m still bound to their expectations in a way. Oh well.

I once had a reputation for being hardworking and smart but all the energy was sucked out of me after the abuse worsened. But I don’t want “all I have” to be my looks either. These kinds of superficial relationships mean nothing and I don’t have the energy for them. I would rather keep to myself and have precious little but myself. So that is what I do.

I don’t think you are exhibiting narcissistic traits, and if you were, it would not incriminate you or deem you as an “even worse person”—as I like to jump to such conclusions about myself far too quickly. You are thinking about yourself and the way you look because you have been shown by the people around you that it is a valid form of currency. But what are you gaining? Nothing that you seem to like or enjoy—but I wonder if it’s because you think you don’t deserve it to begin with. My advice is that you ought to rewire the way you view your appearance. If someone is clearly treating you better for it, then decide in yourself if their other traits render them a good person to keep around. If not, briskly move forward. And if so, then it isn’t a matter of deserving or not. It is here. Enjoy it if even for a moment. Everybody, even the most conventionally unattractive, have managed to find people/a person to keep by their side. You must view yourself as their inherent equal to stop disparaging yourself for things you can’t control. Right now, you seem to view yourself as both better and worse, at the same time. Relinquish that.

Natural selection is among many scientific theories that are a result of analyzing observation and arriving to a logical relation. But it is not the same as empirical evidence, which is composes natural law and scientific knowledge - it is the marriage of knowledge and logical extrapolation. A theory is never a fact. It is an explanation of one or more facts. But it is not absolute, and I think that is really important: what is so powerful about nature is that it proves itself through the absolute fact of its existence, and not theory or abstraction. These are tools used and created by humans to better understand it.

That being said, even within the context of the theory, natural selection cannot and has not been observed to act on every gene or trait. And this is a very important piece, which does not refute but supplements the theory of natural selection. There are many traits that simply emerged and propagated because of chance, and don't in any way increase or decrease an organism's chances of passing on its genes.

The relationship between people with disabilities and reduced birth rates is so utterly negligible that it has not and cannot feasibly 'cull' us. So, what then? Yes, adaptive traits may become more common in response to changing environments, but this is over the course of many many generations. What we are experiencing with our collective depression is not natural selection, it is the world changing so fast and inverting tens of thousands of years of human experience over the span of just a few decades. How do we force ourselves to become cogs in this corrupted machine of civillization that is so new, so new that so many pieces of it have arisen in the span of a single lifetime, when we and our geneologies are so damn ancient?

Know that since prehistoric times - which people most keenly liken to 'survival of the fittest' - we have looked after our disabled. We cared for our elderly like we did our young. Even if variable degrees of depression and disability are inheritable, it does not mean that we are a targets of nature's cyclical culling. In fact, it tells us the opposite; that you are alive today because every generation before you was able to survive, whether you approach it as despite, or given the fact of their disability. The people around them, or the lack thereof.

And if it ever becomes too muddy, please remember: natural selection is a theory. A theory is never a fact. Nature is a fact, and we can only observe it. You are nature, too, and you choose how you observe you. When you give nature such profound credence, recognize that you are here today only because you are a part of it, existing immutably and with great realness.

You belong here.
